Arnold encouraged the listener’s suggested third-level reading of fatherless and widow imagery but declined to comment further. His brief encouragement is not expanded into a fully developed interpretation.

Arnold cited Ezekiel 28:17–18 and Matthew 10:28 and described final destruction as ceasing to exist rather than endless conscious torment. He also said remembrance would end. These are his interpretations.

Arnold said to order them in Christ’s name to return to where they came from, describing the wrong side of the gulf. He used the swine episode as an illustration and distinguished evil spiritual influence from the Holy Spirit. This is his religious explanation, not a diagnosis of a person’s experiences.
Arnold reassured the eight-year-old that an evil spirit could not confuse God, describing God as supreme and supernatural.

Arnold attributed that to lack of teachers and scholars and connected it with his interpretation of Revelation’s approved churches. His accusations about ancestry and religious groups are unverified doctrinal claims and do not establish modern people’s lineage.

Arnold directed the listener to Genesis 11 and interpreted the tower as an attempt at self-provided protection after the flood. He extended the warning to a hypothetical attempt at immortality through cloning; that extension is his speculation, not established science.

Arnold recommended discernment and gently sharing a small point with someone receptive, following up if they asked more. He warned against trying to correct whole churches and said only God could make the seed grow.

Arnold explicitly declined to answer for other churches. He instead discussed Easter as a translation choice in Acts and contrasted it with Passover. His reply should not be expanded into a claim about other churches’ motives.

Arnold interpreted the forehead as belief in false Messiah and the right hand as doing his work. He connected that with supporting false teaching and used Mark 13’s childbirth imagery symbolically. These are his interpretations.

Arnold said help for relatives on the other side of the gulf must await the millennium and referred to Ezekiel 44:25. He allowed helping as many as desired but mentioned a temporary cost, which he considered worthwhile; he did not say their state could be changed immediately after death.

Arnold clarified that by no humans he meant no flesh bodies. He said all change into spiritual bodies at the final trumpet and connected millennium instruction with the spiritually dead awaiting the later resurrection. His wording does not mean the people themselves cease to exist.

Arnold identified the elect as teachers and the rest of the spiritually dead as learners in his millennium interpretation. He distinguished being taught and tested from a second chance for someone already given a genuine opportunity.

Arnold described Egypt as used in God’s purposes and as a place of safety for Jesus’ family under threat. A named servant is inaudible in the captions. His additional prediction and historical claim about Egypt’s continuous nationhood are attributed, not independently verified.

Arnold distinguished a later opportunity to learn from a second chance, arguing that some people had not been taught truth and discussing Romans 11’s stupor language. He said spiritual bodies would remove flesh limitations, while leaving the choice to individuals. This is his doctrinal account.

Arnold reassured the listener who needed to support herself and her family, using the ox-in-the-ditch illustration. He emphasized that she was still studying Scripture rather than treating necessary weekend work as an automatic sin.

Arnold declined to decide Judas’s final standing, leaving judgment to God. He referred to Acts 1:18 and repeated his interpretation that others killed Judas to silence him. That accusation is his interpretation, not an independently established account.

Arnold distinguished limited recreation spending from compulsive gambling that consumes food or housing money. He allowed personal recreation spending only when it did not deprive the family and was not a habit the person could not resist. This records his pastoral distinction.
Arnold emphatically rejected that conclusion and urged the listener not to assume guilt. He used Luke 13 and the tower of Siloam to distinguish an accident from a measure of the victims’ sin.

Arnold connected Jacob and Esau with his first-earth-age interpretation and Esau’s disregard for his inheritance. He also claimed birth circumstances were earned in that earlier age, while emphasizing change through Christ. That claim is his doctrine and does not establish anyone’s worth or responsibility for hardship. His captioned Romans chapter number remains uncertain.

Arnold denied giants were aboard in the account he described, while claiming other human peoples, including Kenites, were included under two of every flesh. These are his interpretations; the answer must not be presented as established ancestry of modern populations.

Arnold explained mother of all living through Christ’s descent from Eve and the eternal life he associated with Christ, rather than making her the genealogical mother of every people. He said humans he called sixth-day creation could sin without attributing their actions to Eve. His ancestry account is doctrinal interpretation.

Arnold directed the listener to Daniel 10 and 12, described Michael as Israel’s chief prince and God’s servant, and rejected identifying Michael as Christ. He warned against angel worship and distinguished archangels from Christ’s birth through a woman.

Arnold approved jury service as a biblical responsibility, describing peers deciding from facts and corroborating witnesses. He distinguished that task from the spiritual judgment he told listeners to leave to God. This is his religious answer, not legal advice.

Arnold located Christianity’s origin in Christ and described Christians as people who worship and follow him. He pointed to followers in Mark’s account rather than giving a historical chronology of later institutions.

Arnold described recognizing that false Christ comes first and intending to stand against him as a strong indication of election in his teaching. He said it did not make a person special and linked others’ lack of understanding with Romans 11’s stupor language and millennium instruction.

In a second listener’s question, Arnold again claimed Kenites were included under two of every flesh aboard the ark. He gave a tentative Genesis chapter-and-verse reference whose wording needs review. This additional answer stays linked but does not count the same recording twice for this question. His claim is doctrinal interpretation.

Arnold reassured the listener by limiting the unpardonable sin, in his interpretation, to the elect refusing the Holy Spirit’s testimony when delivered before false Messiah. He distinguished that future situation from past cursing and urged repentance rather than lifelong fear.
Arnold reassured the listener that studying Scripture through the televised Chapel service counted as being in church. He said God did not hold inability to travel against a disabled person.

Arnold pointed to Ezekiel 13 following verse 20 and applied its flying imagery against rapture teaching. He criticized newer translations and alleged scribal interference. Those translation accusations and the prophetic application are his claims, not independently verified textual conclusions.

Arnold said Satan considered himself convincing and successful in attracting followers. He connected numbers and force with his reading of Daniel 11, rather than saying knowledge of an eventual end would stop the deception.

Arnold interpreted trumpets as recognizable events rather than sounds listeners would hear. He distinguished understanding the seals, recognizing what each trumpet describes, and the pouring out of wrath. These are his prophetic interpretations.

Arnold read 1 Thessalonians 4:13–17 in the context of those already dead being with Christ. He interpreted air as spiritual life and clouds as a large company, placing the change into spiritual bodies at the last trumpet. These lexical and prophetic readings are attributed to him, not independently verified translations.

Arnold distinguished the horsemen as conditions, identifying the first white-horse rider with antichrist, from the four bound angels whom he called fallen angels. He said the latter had a future task; he did not identify the two groups as the same.

Arnold said horses were unclean in his dietary-law teaching because their hooves were not divided. He also expressed his personal reluctance as a rancher to eat a horse. This is his religious dietary answer.

Arnold described the bound angels as fallen angels restrained after departing from God’s plan. He connected their restraint with Jude’s opening verses and repeated his interpretation linking angelic seduction with Noah’s flood.

Arnold said it was possible they would begin their activity before the two witnesses appeared. He urged watchfulness, without stating a certain date or treating that possibility as a confirmed sequence.

Arnold emphasized that Naomi did not yet fully recognize the blessing of Ruth remaining with her. He connected Ruth and Boaz with Christ’s lineage and said Naomi eventually recognized her blessing. He did not endorse the listener’s threat of punishment for Naomi.

Arnold interpreted the forehead as belief in false Messiah and the hand as helping his work. He connected that with his reading of the first person taken in Matthew 24 and Mark 13 as deceived by false Christ. These are his interpretations.

Arnold explicitly treated the phrase spiritually: resisting fleshly appetites and following the inward spiritual person. He used Christ’s temptation as an example and referred to two bodies in 1 Corinthians 15. He was not instructing bodily injury. A conflicting flesh-return clause in the captions remains held.

Arnold urged repentance, a change of heart and asking forgiveness after backsliding. He used Paul’s earlier persecution of Christians to reassure the listener that serious wrongdoing need not prevent repentance. His captioned chosen-vessel citation needs checking; it is not silently corrected.

Arnold recommended Mark 13, emphasizing purpose, a role in God’s plan and the Holy Spirit’s testimony. He suggested that seeing themselves addressed by Scripture would encourage the children to study. This is his pastoral application.

Arnold said no. He described English translations as usable and Strong’s Concordance as an optional way to investigate Hebrew, Greek and Aramaic meanings. He distinguished deeper language study from loving Christ and trusting the price he paid.

Arnold denied a physical marriage and interpreted betrothal and marriage language spiritually. He also treated God’s divorce imagery for Israel as analogy, referring tentatively to Jeremiah 3:7 or 8. His account of unnamed writings and translators is attributed rather than independently verified.
Arnold located his explanation in Ezekiel 28, interpreted Tyrus as the false rock and said Satan had earned the former protecting-cherub role. These are his lexical and doctrinal interpretations.

Arnold described italics as marking words supplied by translators to carry the sense into English. He urged care with such additions and recommended reading the translators’ prefatory letter and consulting the Companion Bible.

Arnold assumed the conscious father had probably requested anointing and gave reassurance on that basis. He also said listeners must not judge the man and that God knew his thoughts. His pastoral inference should not be turned into a guarantee that anointing automatically proves repentance.

Arnold recommended Companion Bible Appendix 179, his Christmas study and Luke 1’s priestly-course material. The captioned calendar terminology is damaged, so its date calculation is not reconstructed or presented as established chronology.

Arnold said a mature Christian could regard clean meat as unaffected by an idol, but should abstain when eating it would offend or mislead a less mature believer. His emphasis was care for the weaker believer rather than unrestricted permission to ignore others.

Arnold rejected the reported claim that the people disappeared after AD 70. He cited Matthew 10:6 and James’s opening address to scattered tribes. This response supplied biblical references, not independent proof of the identity of modern nations.

Arnold distinguished his proposed third earth age from the present age and said angels in the latter could have gender. He connected fallen angels with his Genesis seduction interpretation and treated resurrection marriage language separately. These are his doctrinal claims, not established accounts of human reproduction.

Arnold attributed the destruction of his proposed first earth age to Satan’s pride and drawing a third of God’s children away. He referred to Ezekiel 28:18–19. This is his interpretation of an earlier age.

Arnold said there were animal bodies but no human flesh bodies in that earlier age. He gave approximate dates and claimed mammoth carbon dating supported his chronology. Those dating and scientific claims are his assertions, not independently established evidence.

Arnold distinguished a Passover high Sabbath from the weekly Sabbath and placed the crucifixion and burial before Wednesday sunset. He referred to a Companion Bible appendix for a detailed count. The captioned sequence repeats a day number, so the full hour-by-hour calculation remains unresolved rather than silently repaired.

Arnold said he could not tell how serious the reported lying was and did not approve it. He suggested setting a good example, referred to 1 Corinthians 7 and qualified his reassurance with the behavior not involving very serious matters. His answer was based on limited details.

Arnold allowed long hair and interpreted the covering principally as Christ’s protection. He connected 1 Corinthians 11:6 and 10 with his reading of returning fallen angels and Noah’s days in Matthew 24. He explicitly identified part of that connection as his own wording.

Arnold named Huldah and Deborah and suggested looking up prophetess in Strong’s Concordance. He cited 2 Kings 22:14. His later identification of the father of four prophesying daughters is uncertain in the captions and is not corrected or endorsed here.

Arnold described the soul as the person’s self or being, retaining identity through a change of body. He appealed to Matthew’s warning about the soul perishing, while also calling it eternal. That tension remains flagged; his answer is not rewritten as an unqualified claim that a soul cannot perish.
scripture_mentions: Matthew, warning about body and soul

occurrences.summary: Arnold answered the two-creation question by saying Satan deceived people generally and that no person was perfect. He did not trace a genetic transmission of Adam and Eve’s wrongdoing or provide a detailed mechanism in this reply.

Arnold explicitly said shortening the witnesses’ time was not written, then inferred a balanced relationship with the shortened opposing period from God’s fairness. His solar-day/lunar-month comparison is unclear and remains held. The inference is not presented as an explicit biblical timetable.

Arnold rejected that claim, referred to the fish account in John 21 and distinguished someone choosing vegetarianism from claiming Jesus practiced it. He qualified his approval of meat with his clean-food interpretation.

Arnold referred the listener to the address announced at the program’s end and thanked her for supporting the teaching. This records the broadcast’s contact response; it does not independently verify current contact details.

Arnold tentatively suggested 1 Corinthians 6:2 as the passage the listener might mean, but explicitly said it did not quite say what she had described. He did not affirm the proposed automatic exemption from later judgment.

Arnold advised telling the three-year-old truth at a level suited to her understanding, keeping it simple and avoiding invented stories. He recommended the children’s study book as help in approaching difficult subjects, while noting that children develop differently.

Arnold praised the family’s abstinence, urged resisting temptation and framed their purpose through Mark 13 and his teaching about spiritual opposition. He suggested prayer and anointing. This records pastoral encouragement rather than a clinical addiction-treatment plan.

Arnold said fleshly weakness could still tempt believers and emphasized following the inward spiritual person. He added that no one was perfect and that people sometimes fell short and needed forgiveness. He did not promise automatic freedom from temptation.

Arnold rejected universal salvation, distinguished spiritual bodies from mortal or immortal souls in his interpretation, and referred to Revelation 20’s final judgment. He also said listeners must not decide individual destinies. The question’s five-month premise after seeing Christ was not clearly resolved in this response.

Arnold referred to Revelation 9 and especially verse 4 for his teaching that the period was five months and those sealed were protected. He denied that believers were helpless and connected their testimony with Mark 13, Matthew 24 and Luke 21.

Arnold connected election with Ephesians 1:4, his proposed first-age stand against Satan and divine intercession in Romans 8:26 onward. He described recognizing false Christ’s prior appearance and intending to witness against him as an indication of election. These are his doctrinal interpretations.

Arnold used Daniel 5’s writing on the wall as an example he found humorous, describing the ruler’s fear after misusing the sacred vessels. His added description of the reaction is his interpretation rather than a verified literal translation.
Arnold denied that an unbaptized infant would go to hell. He distinguished blessing or christening a baby from baptism chosen by someone able to understand and accept responsibility.

Arnold pointed to the Companion Bible commentary alongside Daniel 7:8 for names and roles he associated with Satan, including the little horn, antichrist and the serpent. This records his proposed identifications.

Arnold distinguished Christ’s arrival at the millennium’s beginning and cleansing of Zion from the consuming fire and second death at its end. He described the intervening period as teaching with Satan restrained. His precise captioned priesthood verse reference needs checking.

Arnold recommended 2 Timothy 2:15 and explained rightly dividing as attending to speaker or audience, subject, context and time period. He preferred sustained chapter-and-verse study to building an entire message around an isolated verse.
Arnold said ashes to ashes was not a biblical phrase and referred to Ecclesiastes 12:6–7 for the return to dust and spirit. He explicitly said his point did not forbid cremation.

Arnold distinguished false from true Christ by his sixth-then-seventh-trumpet sequence. He said false Christ deceives people who expect to be taken away, whereas Christ returns at the seventh trumpet. These are his prophetic interpretations.

Arnold tentatively suggested 1 Timothy 4:3 and opposed others judging marriage or food. He added an unclear qualification about marrying someone God created to be received. That limitation remains unresolved rather than expanded into a rule he did not explicitly explain.

Arnold cited Leviticus 20:11 and 18:8 and interpreted Ham’s offense as intercourse with his father’s wife, rather than merely seeing Noah unclothed. This is his interpretation of the Genesis account; the legal passages are the references he supplied.

Arnold directed the listener to Revelation 20 beginning with verse 10, leading into the great white throne judgment. He said genuinely repented sins were erased through Christ and distinguished them from righteous acts bringing reward.

Arnold placed Christ’s return and the change into spiritual bodies at the seventh trumpet, which he called the millennium’s first day. He described the millennium as an opportunity for people previously unable to understand, followed by Satan’s brief release and a test. This is his prophetic interpretation.

Arnold read being delivered to death as being delivered to the devil, connecting Hebrews 2:14 with his identification of Satan as antichrist. He appealed to Luke 21’s protection language and 2 Thessalonians 2:4, reasoning that a figure impersonating Jesus would expose himself by butchering people. This is his interpretation of Matthew 24:9.
Arnold first said 2 Peter 3:6, then audibly corrected himself to verse 8 and recommended reading verses 6–8 for the day-and-thousand-years comparison. The correction is retained.

Arnold discussed the book of life, Christ’s judgment seat and the rich man and Lazarus in Luke 16. He said earthly church records were not the authoritative heavenly record. He did not directly locate a passage describing pearly gates in this answer.

Arnold pointed to Ecclesiastes 12:6 and interpreted the broken silver cord as death. He described the chapter’s images of aging and said the spiritual person returns to the Father while the flesh returns to dust.

Arnold assumed the listener meant the Holy Spirit and said God’s Spirit was for whoever would receive it, including in Old Testament times. He described Israel’s role in bringing the word and Messiah to others, then cited Ezekiel 18:4 to emphasize that all souls belong to God.

Arnold recommended Luke 10:19, interpreting it as authority over evil spirits and Satan. He urged accepting that authority and anointing oneself and the home. He did not separately explain the listener’s phrase about taking every thought captive.

Arnold described a separate eighth-day formation of Adam and Eve after sixth-day humanity and seventh-day rest, assigning it the task of tending the soil and bringing forth Christ. He said that lineage continued, and corrected the listener’s reversed comparison of a day with God and a thousand human years. These are his creation and chronology interpretations.

Arnold opposed drawing wings on angels and interpreted Ezekiel 1’s imagery as flying vehicles of polished bronze. He also distinguished Christ’s image from the plural our image, which he took as addressing spiritual beings. These are his interpretations, not independently verified descriptions of angels or vehicles.

Asked about John 5:28–29, Arnold connected it with people appearing after Christ’s death and said they were spiritual rather than flesh bodies, visible as evidence that Christ defeated death. His example of a local shopkeeper was an illustration, not a named biblical person. The connection between the question’s passage and his explanation remains flagged.

Arnold predicted Americans would vote out officials who removed the motto and restore it. This was his opinion in the saved broadcast, not a guarantee about current or future policy. His demographic claim was not independently verified.

Asked about Daniel 12:1–2, Arnold described Michael as Israel’s protecting archangel and as restraining Satan. He referred to Revelation 12:6–7 and anticipated Satan and his angels being cast down as part of his false-messiah teaching. He did not separately explain Daniel 12:2’s resurrection language.

Arnold referred to Romans 11’s spirit of slumber to explain why some people would not receive a witness. He explicitly presented waiting until the millennium as his own thought, advised planting a seed without forcing acceptance and said only God could make it grow.

Arnold associated intoxicating drugs and alcohol with spiritual danger, but also explicitly said there was no shame in seeking outside help for addiction. He recommended prayer and Scripture while thanking places that help people with drug and alcohol problems. This is pastoral advice, not a medical explanation of addiction.
Arnold distinguished daily prayer about problems from chanting and answered that prayer and thanksgiving could both be appropriate. He did not treat the listener’s repeated request as chanting.
Arnold interpreted meek as humble before God: seeking his leadership, listening and trying to do right rather than acting superior. He distinguished sincere effort from pretending to fool God.

Arnold advised finding foundation in Matthew 13 around verses 35–36, tracing it through Strong’s to the root he called kataballo and number 2598, and consulting Companion Bible appendix 146. He connected it with his first-earth-age reading of Jeremiah 4. These are his lexical and doctrinal interpretations.

Arnold interpreted Luke 16’s torment as shame and disappointment rather than physical torture. He corrected his own initial wording to say the suffering was mental, and linked it to his millennium teaching about those who had not understood.

Arnold spoke of Christians looking forward to being with the Lord, but urged praying for the Father’s will because the person might still have work to do. The captions leave the medical detail unfinished; no transplant or treatment claim is supplied here.

Arnold placed Jeremiah 4:23–26 in his proposed first earth age and Isaiah 24:1 in a future shaking at the end of the present age. He also referred to the closing verses of Hebrews 12. These are his chronological interpretations.

Arnold denied saying a murderer could never be forgiven. He cited 1 John 3:15 for his distinction between forgiveness in flesh and God’s later judgment, and distinguished lying-in-wait murder from a crime of passion. This records his doctrine and interpretation, not current legal advice.

Arnold said Christ did not change the law and discussed debt service and release in Leviticus 25, first citing around verses 30–39 and then verse 39 onward. His response focused on debt service and did not address every form of slavery raised by the listener. His generalization is preserved as his claim, not endorsed as a complete historical account.

Arnold urged knowing the subject, preparation and discernment, while being willing to say I do not know and research the answer. He encouraged sharing what one did understand and learning together rather than pretending to know everything.

Arnold said people were still in flesh bodies and interpreted the shortened days as protection from a convincing false Christ. He contrasted the shortened period with seven years and said he expected the elect to withstand deception. These are his prophetic interpretations.

Arnold said it had never been in the United States and claimed it had been hidden in Canada during World War II before being returned. This records an unverified historical assertion from the broadcast, not an established travel history of the stone.

Arnold said spiritual discernment and their supernatural character would identify them. He interpreted 1 Corinthians 11:10 as keeping Christ’s protection because of fallen angels. This is his doctrinal interpretation, not a method for identifying real people as nonhuman.

Arnold recommended Matthew 24 for signs of the end and connected Mark 13’s fig-tree imagery with Israel becoming a nation in 1948. He used that interpretation to call the broadcast’s generation the final one. This is his prophetic interpretation rather than a verified timetable.

Arnold rejected the claim that mere disbelief was the unpardonable sin. He distinguished his murder-forgiveness teaching from God’s final judgment, then interpreted Luke 12:10 as an informed elect person refusing the Holy Spirit’s testimony. These are his doctrinal distinctions; the related murder answer is retained separately.

Drawing on his wartime experience, Arnold emphasized love from home. He mentioned homemade cookies as welcome but said a mother’s love mattered more. This was personal encouragement to a parent of a deployed service member.

Arnold agreed that Ezekiel 18 did not contain the teaching the listener described, and corrected the reference to Ezekiel 13 beginning at verse 18. He interpreted its kerchief and pillow imagery as concealing God’s salvation and teaching people to fly to save their souls. The reference correction and his interpretation are both retained.

Arnold explained the shared morning imagery by describing Satan as an imitator of Christ. He connected this with Satan’s former cherub role and ambition to occupy the mercy seat. This is his interpretation, rather than a detailed translation of the listener’s proposed name meaning.
Arnold explicitly rejected the listener’s proposed identification with Adam and identified the figure as Satan, whom he called Lucifer. This records his interpretation of Isaiah 14:12.

Arnold distinguished John the Baptist from the disciple associated with the Gospel, three epistles and Revelation. He called the latter a scribe and attributed the writings’ ultimate authorship to God, emphasizing inspiration rather than identifying John the Baptist as their writer.

Arnold reassured the child that Christ’s protection and the authority he associated with Luke 10:18–19 meant she need not fear evil spirits. He described ghosts as most likely evil spirits. This is his pastoral and doctrinal response.

Arnold cited Deuteronomy 15:6 and 28:12, identified America with the house of Israel and opposed national borrowing. His proposed ancestry and application to modern government are his interpretations, not independently verified history or current financial guidance.

Arnold said Satan had not yet been cast down as the false messiah. He distinguished the freedom described in Job 1:6 from his belief that Satan became restrained after tempting Christ, while Satan’s evil spirit could still act on earth. He connected the future arrival with Revelation 12 and five months.

Arnold interpreted the Corinthians instruction he mentioned as prohibiting chatter rather than requiring complete silence. He said he prohibited chatter by anyone and also opposed chanting as putting flesh into worship. These are his interpretation and ministry practice.
scripture_mentions: Corinthians, passage not precisely numbered in this answer

occurrences.summary: Arnold said God knows people’s thoughts and cannot be deceived, so he can judge accurately. He contrasted that with human courts’ ability to make mistakes. He did not separately develop the child’s second question about why Satan impersonates God.

Arnold said Satan had no wings to conceal. He explained wing imagery through his interpretation of Ezekiel 1:4 as a metallic vehicle carrying God’s throne. These are his descriptions and lexical claims, not independently verified accounts of spacecraft.

Arnold read Revelation 3:10 as protection from being tempted by false Christ rather than removal from earth. He urged reading 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14 before verses 16–17, interpreting the passage through the dead already being with God and a seventh-trump change of body. His translation claim about air is his interpretation.

Arnold directed the listener to Luke 10:18 and emphasized standing in Christ’s name rather than being afraid. His Greek-word explanation is retained as a claim requiring checking, without silently moving his stated reference to another verse.

Arnold said an innocent child would be fine and described antichrist as arriving in the role of a savior rather than openly attacking children. He warned that the danger he had in mind was deception and loss of the soul. This is his prophetic interpretation.
Arnold cited Revelation 19:8 and described white linen as woven through righteous acts. He used lack of clothing as an image for lacking those acts. This is his explanation of the passage.

Arnold said spiritual bodies do not age and appear young, referring generally to young figures seen at Christ’s tomb. He also said all were of the same age from his proposed first earth age. He did not give a precise numerical age.

Arnold cited Revelation 8:3–4 and said God hears, retains and receives the saints’ prayers, using vial or bottle imagery. This is the reference he gave; the wording is not silently moved to another passage.

Arnold encouraged gratitude for the mother having given the listener life and urged recognizing her illness rather than reducing her to her actions. His suggestion about bodily imbalances was a tentative pastoral explanation, not a diagnosis. The answer did not provide crisis-care instructions.
Arnold said people could name what they remembered, but that asking forgiveness for all their sins was sufficient when they could not remember everything.

Arnold first said most likely, then qualified that believers would know the two witnesses while the whole world would not necessarily recognize who they were. His qualification is retained rather than turning it into universal recognition.

Arnold said the Holy Spirit would make their speech understood in every language at once, and connected that with the future testimony in Mark 13. He did not explicitly confirm the listener’s proposed names, Moses and Elijah, in this reply.

Answering a ten-year-old about heaven, Arnold said spiritual bodies appear young and have no illness, pain or suffering. He linked them with his first-earth-age teaching rather than a numerical earthly age.

Arnold denied a distinction based on some souls being older, saying all came from his proposed first earth age. He recommended Proverbs 8 and Job 38 and treated Wisdom and the rejoicing sons of God as support for that interpretation.

Arnold comforted the bereaved grandmother by saying her granddaughter was with the Father and would appear as a young adult in a spiritual body. He described that as the enduring body rather than a child growing up in heaven. These are his doctrinal assurances.

Arnold referred to Isaiah 11’s peaceful animals and said God would keep animals in the millennium. He treated the child imagery as a statement of safety and denied carnivory because he expected no flesh. These are his interpretations, not a proof about every individual pet.

Arnold rejected a rapture and placed the gathering with Christ on earth after the seventh-trump change into spiritual bodies. He referred to Revelation 21 and anticipated testimony in Mark 13, assuring believers of protection. This is his prophetic interpretation.

Arnold assumed the listener meant Revelation 19:8 and corrected religious to righteous. He described doing right, loving God and planting a seed as examples, connecting these acts with the linen imagery.

Arnold rejected the labels and emphasized individual responsibility and judgment. He acknowledged the disciples pooling finances but explained that through their traveling ministry. His generalizations about modern political systems were his opinions, not an independent political or historical assessment.

Arnold said a person could accept what came to them without worshiping antichrist, and placed the line at a demand for worship in his predicted world system. This records his prophetic distinction, not a finding about any present benefits program.

Arnold opposed putting large savings into hidden gold or silver, suggested only a small amount for liquidity or barter and said the rest should be kept safely. He explicitly disliked giving financial advice. His broadcast-era allocation suggestion is not presented as current investment guidance.

Arnold rejected the idea of people remaining in graves until God bursts them open, saying the flesh returns to dust and the person returns to God in a spiritual body. He cited 2 Corinthians 5:7–8. A separate captioned John 8 reference accompanying God of the living language remains flagged rather than corrected.

Arnold restricted Genesis 9:19’s spreading language to the Adamic lineage in his interpretation, while claiming other peoples were also aboard the ark under every flesh. He connected this with his sixth-day creation, Kenite and fallen-angel teachings and 1 Chronicles 2:55. These are his ancestry and flood interpretations, not established accounts of human origins.

Arnold associated Smyrna and Philadelphia with the churches Christ approved and interpreted the passage as delivery before Satan followed by the Holy Spirit’s testimony. He urged the listener not to worry and to seek peace in the family. This is his prophetic interpretation.

Arnold told the listener that studying with the broadcast counted as being in church and gathering in the Spirit, regardless of location. He did not require physical attendance as proof of being Christian in this answer.
Arnold said antichrist would arrange transport, speculating about supernatural powers and fantastic vehicles. He offered no practical travel plan or independent evidence for that mechanism.

Arnold predicted widespread headlines claiming Christ had returned because of supernatural signs and an apparently peaceful, prosperous arrival. He distinguished that sixth-trump figure from true Christ. These are his prophetic expectations, not a report of an actual event.

Arnold said advising a loved one in the millennium would not immediately move that person to the other side. He required the person’s own stand against Satan after the millennium and connected it with the second resurrection in Revelation 20. He also distinguished the second death. This is his interpretation.

Arnold said repentance washes away past sins and used Paul’s former opposition to Christians as an example of a chosen person with serious wrongdoing. He referred to Stephen’s death in Acts 7 and Paul’s Damascus experience in Acts 9 rather than excluding the listener from election because of her past.

Arnold tentatively said probably not, then warned the listener not to judge which side someone occupied. The reported medical circumstances are unclear in the captions; neither a visitation nor its cause is independently verified by this answer.

Arnold understood the letter as asking whether God could forgive. He emphasized repentance and Christ’s death while reserving judgment to God, even when discussing capital punishment. The listener’s precise question was not fully read aloud, and the reply does not determine the person’s legal or final spiritual outcome.

Arnold directed the listener to 1 Timothy 5:8 and paraphrased its warning as being worse than an infidel when a person refuses to care for their own family. He did not develop detailed exceptions or limits in this short reply.
Arnold answered yes to the listener’s proposed connection between Michael casting Satan from heaven and Satan’s sixth-trump arrival. This is his prophetic chronology.

Arnold said Satan’s confinement in the abyss during the millennium would prevent every kind of influence, explicitly including his evil spirit. He distinguished this total restraint from the influence he allowed at other times.

Arnold recommended Mark 13 and Jeremiah 24, and linked the good and bad figs with his interpretation of Israel’s establishment. He also traced fig leaves back to his seduction reading of Eden. These are his connected interpretations, not independently verified history.

Arnold urged not judging the brother, tentatively took his Bible reading and questions as encouraging signs and mentioned possible help in the millennium. His reassurance was based on a short letter, not a verified judgment of the deceased person.

Arnold distinguished spoken prayers, which he said Satan could hear, from silent prayers known to God. He also advised discretion about important plans for serving God because he expected opposition. This records his teaching about spiritual knowledge.

Arnold recommended planting small seeds, answering follow-up questions and avoiding presenting everything at once. He illustrated this with his America-as-Israel interpretation, but also said to keep loving relatives who did not receive it. His example’s ancestry claim remains his interpretation.

Arnold pointed to Genesis 8:21 and 9:13, interpreting the rainbow as a reminder of God’s covenant, and mentioned Isaiah 54. He also made a climate claim about recent cooling; that broadcast-era assertion is not independently verified here.

Arnold treated the verse as a warning against persuasive false teaching. He encouraged a working knowledge of Scripture through sustained study, without requiring every listener to have a pastor’s level of skill.

Arnold said no, claiming there were fewer Kenites than the one-third group in his first-age teaching and identifying the term with Cain’s offspring. His population estimates and arithmetic are unclear and remain held. These are his ancestry claims, not established facts about any modern population.

Arnold said the people he called Kenites had the same opportunity for redemption through a change of heart and love of the Lord. He emphasized that God created all souls and called redeemed people God’s children. This records his doctrinal response without endorsing his ancestry classification.

Arnold inferred that something in his proposed first earth age explained birth into the ancestry he called Kenite, appealing to God’s fairness rather than giving a specific event. He also said salvation remained available to all peoples. His inference is not verified genealogy or a basis for judging present-day people.

Arnold affirmed that adoptive relationships count as family and used Joseph’s relationship with Jesus as his example. He connected this with Ezekiel 44:20–25. A damaged qualification near the answer’s end remains unresolved; it is not expanded into an exclusion of either adoptive or birth parents.

Arnold recommended Mark 13 for his teaching that false Christ appears before true Christ, followed by Christ’s coming and the millennium on earth. He connected that expectation with Jerusalem and the day’s Isaiah lesson. This is his prophetic interpretation.

Arnold directed the listener to Leviticus 11 and summarized his dietary teaching as avoiding scavengers. The question was cut short on air. His assurance about health is a religious dietary claim, not a medical guarantee.

Arnold described final destruction as ceasing to exist and being forgotten, relating that to the absence of tears. He pointed to Psalm 37 and claimed an acrostic supported his reading. His additional Revelation 22 reference remains unverified rather than being silently replaced. These are his interpretations.

Arnold read Ezekiel 40 onward as the millennium with people in spiritual bodies. He inferred recognition of loved ones from his reading of Ezekiel 44:20–25 as permitting help to relatives. This is the reasoning he supplied, not an explicit quotation saying all family members recognize each other.

Arnold said any Christian could baptize another Christian, while acknowledging that some churches impose their own membership requirements. He described baptism as a public statement of belief in Christ’s death, burial and resurrection. He also mentioned baptism at ministry gatherings without verifying present availability.

Arnold rejected a rapture reading of 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and urged reading from verse 13. He interpreted cloud as a group and air as a spiritual life body, connecting this with Hebrews 12 and a last-trump change. His lexical claims and historical allegation about rapture teaching are his assertions, not independently verified findings.

Arnold encouraged repentance and trust in Christ’s redemption when repayment was genuinely impossible. He acknowledged restitution when possible and reassured the listener about forgiveness. His answer concerns spiritual forgiveness and does not determine or cancel legal debts.

Arnold said souls not yet born were with the Father but explicitly declined to guess which side of the gulf they occupied. He also asserted that the end could not come before every soul had an opportunity for flesh birth. The limitation on his knowledge is retained.

Arnold said repentance frees a person from past wrongdoing, while reserving deliberate criminal homicide for God’s judgment. He distinguished it from accidents and crimes of passion. This is his doctrinal qualification rather than a determination of any individual’s final outcome.

Arnold recommended gentle conversation, planting a seed and showing a happy example rather than overwhelming the sister. He suggested Mark 13 and referred to possible help in the millennium through his Ezekiel 44 interpretation. He did not independently verify the reported spirits.

Arnold declined to judge the listener’s former church but identified antichrist as Satan, the son of perdition claiming to be God. He cited 2 Thessalonians 2:2–4, especially verse 4, and Ezekiel 28:18–19. The listener’s earlier-teaching question was unclear; this records the identification he actually gave.

Arnold interpreted winter as being harvested spiritually out of season by false Christ. He separately explained the Sabbath warning through restricted travel distance and said the elect would remain as witnesses. These are his readings of Mark 13 and Matthew 24.
Arnold explained the title as referring to Christ’s life in a human flesh body. He connected it with John 1’s account of the Word becoming flesh.

Arnold directed the listener to Luke 16:26 and distinguished an initial placement on either side of paradise’s gulf from the later great white throne judgment after the millennium. He related the placement to the book of life. This is his interpretation.

Challenged because instantly was absent from the passage, Arnold defended an immediate return of the spirit by reasoning from the silver cord breaking. He described aging and the body returning to dust. His answer offers an interpretation of the timing, not evidence that the English word instantly appears in those verses.

Arnold said the elect entered flesh to guide and help others, while distinguishing groups with differing responses in his proposed first earth age. He linked divine intercession and prior justification with Romans 8 and Ephesians 1:4. These are his interpretations rather than verified accounts of prehuman existence.

Arnold described the Chapel’s pattern of communion at Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles rather than every meeting. He opposed treating it as an empty ritual but also permitted Christians to partake at other times when they needed strength.

Arnold explicitly allowed a family to take communion at home and said any Christian could partake. He mentioned illness, discouragement and a need for strength as occasions, without restricting it to a scheduled church gathering.

Arnold interpreted the silver cord as life leaving the flesh and the bowl as the body sustained from earthly material. He referred to Ecclesiastes 9 and 1 Corinthians 15:35 onward for his distinction between flesh and spiritual bodies. His broad claim that nonorganic substances are harmful is not endorsed as medical or nutritional guidance.

Arnold said unborn souls were enjoying being with the Father and asserted that all must be born of woman before the end. He referred generally to the Apocrypha without naming a book or passage; that claim is not supplied with an invented citation.

Arnold treated baptism in Jesus’ name and in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit as equivalent, explaining Jesus as Savior and describing his own threefold wording. The Matthew reference and sacred-name words are damaged in the captions, so no corrected verse or reconstructed pronunciation is supplied.

Arnold clarified that Deuteronomy 31’s final verse identifies the song and that the song itself is in chapter 32. He also connected it with overcomers singing in Revelation 15, first saying around verse 2 and then verse 3.

Arnold said knowing false Christ comes before true Christ and intending to withstand him was probably an indication of election. He acknowledged that everyone sins and that faithful people can still feel fear or anxiety. His probability language is retained rather than certifying the listener’s election.

Arnold agreed that Lazarus’s raising demonstrated Christ’s power over death, then connected the crucifixion and torn temple veil with access to God. His exact captioned Corinthians verse number for the victory-over-death language remains held rather than corrected.

Arnold did not endorse that date. He anticipated attention to December 21, 2012 as well, then urged watching Jerusalem and remaining spiritually alert. He explained Gethsemane’s cup through his wrath interpretation. This records a historical broadcast response, not a current prediction.

Arnold distinguished an initial decision about a person’s side of paradise after death from the great white throne judgment on the millennium’s final day. He said earthly church letters were not the controlling record and emphasized the heavenly book of life.

Arnold inferred continuing consciousness from his reading of the silver cord breaking and returning to the Father. He did not supply a separate verse explicitly using the word consciousness or establish that instantly is printed in the passage.

Arnold referred to man being made in our image and to John 14’s seen me, seen the Father language. He described Christ as God made visible in the dimension of human life. This is his theological explanation, not a physical portrait.

Arnold recommended Luke 10:18–20, commanding evil to leave in Christ’s name and anointing doorposts with olive oil. This records his religious response without independently confirming the listener’s explanation of disturbing experiences.

Arnold said to speak to God plainly, describe the trouble and recall God’s promises. He referred to Ezekiel 18:4, Isaiah 43 around verse 26, James 5 and his dietary reading of Deuteronomy 14 and Leviticus 11. His anointing and diet recommendations are pastoral teaching, not a guarantee of recovery.

Arnold said perhaps not in every case and placed blame and punishment on the fallen angels in his reading of Jude 6. He described hybrid offspring and linked their destruction with the flood. These are his interpretations, not established accounts of human reproduction.

Arnold claimed science and Scripture agreed and used his proposed first earth age to explain ancient creatures and dates. He mentioned carbon dating and other methods without providing measurements or a reproducible comparison. His agreement claim is not independently demonstrated by this reply.

Arnold made the answer depend on whether the person understood the original baptism as a public confession of Christ’s death, burial and resurrection. If she had understood, he regarded her as baptized; otherwise he left the choice to her. Changing churches alone was not his test.

Arnold cited Hosea 14:8 and treated an evergreen as a symbol of enduring life rather than an object of worship. He also repeated his belief that December 25 marked Christ’s conception and recommended the Christmas study. These are his scriptural and calendar interpretations.

Arnold recommended Companion Bible appendix 179 and its discussion of the priestly courses for researching his proposed dates. The listener’s June dates are unclear, and the reply does not itself work through a complete calendar calculation.

Arnold cited Matthew 24:30 and Revelation 11:15, placing Christ’s return at the seventh trumpet after false Christ’s sixth-trump appearance. He distinguished this sequence from a calendar date. These are his prophetic interpretations.

Arnold identified Satan, antichrist and false prophet as one figure operating under several names. He read Revelation 13:11–14’s lamb-like appearance, dragon speech and miracles through that identification. This preserves his interpretation as its own source-bound answer.

Arnold told the listener to request the Chapel’s book list to obtain a Companion Bible. This records instructions in the saved broadcast and does not verify current stock, pricing or ordering arrangements.

Arnold preferred Strong’s for the listener’s translation question while still recommending Green’s as an inexpensive way to consult the underlying texts. He criticized aspects of Green’s translation but the captioned Thessalonians reference and Greek word are damaged. His preference is recorded without independently resolving the disputed entries.

Arnold interpreted golden streets as spiritual purity and mansion as a resting or abiding place, connecting John 14 with God dwelling with believers through the Comforter. He said this rest could be experienced now, while also discussing the millennium and eternity. These are his interpretations.

Arnold encouraged the disabled listener to share small seeds when opportunities arose and answer follow-up questions without overwhelming others. He described her continuing faith as a witness itself and urged gentleness rather than exhausting or hurting herself.

Arnold said those who followed Satan after his short release would face the great white throne judgment and the lake of fire, which he identified as the second death. He directed the listener to the closing verses of Revelation 20.
